2025_126_mscurrguide_24_25.paragraph: The Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025 describes the philosophy, goals, outcomes, and full course catalog for grades 6 through 8 across the district's middle schools. It lays out a three-year scheduling framework in which sixth graders take five academic classes plus every-other-day physical education and an optional every-other-day music or art elective, while seventh and eighth graders take four academic classes plus required Health/Physical Education and Digital Applications 1.0, a full-year music option, and a growing elective load. The most consequential structural feature is that eighth-grade Algebra 1 Honors, Geometry Honors, and World Language I carry high school credit and are figured into the student's high school GPA.
2025_126_mscurrguide_24_25.page:
Overview
The Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025 is an 18-page catalog covering middle school philosophy, goals, student outcomes, a three-year scheduling overview, and course descriptions for grades 6, 7, and 8.

Philosophy, Goals, and Outcomes
Troy middle schools state a commitment to academic excellence and to being developmentally responsive to adolescents' innate curiosity, desire to expand their environment, and need for recognition and personal achievement. The program is characterized by a research-based curriculum with effective assessment and evaluation; a shared vision fostering respect for learning, diversity, and responsible behavior; and a cooperative partnership with parents and community. Goals 1 through 9 cover developmental appropriateness, a diverse student population, core-subject skills, discovery of special interests and aptitudes, diversified cultural/social/civic/vocational/recreational experiences, guidance services promoting self-esteem and independence, community partnerships, transition from elementary to high school, and modeling healthy lifestyles. The stated outcomes are a self-directed learner, a quality worker, a positive communicator, a collaborative and cooperative contributor, and an involved and visionary citizen.

Three-Year Scheduling Overview

| Grade | Academic load | Additional requirements | Elective allowance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | Five academic classes | Physical Education (EOD, required) | Orchestra, Choir, Band, or Art, all EOD |
| 7 | Four academic classes | Health/Physical Education (1/2 year), Digital Applications 1.0 (1/2 year); music students take Concert Band, Chamber Orchestra, or Choir full year | One full year total (two 1/2-year electives or one full-year elective) |
| 8 | Four academic classes | Music students take Symphonic Band, Advanced Orchestra, or Choir full year | Non-music students: two full years total (four 1/2-year classes, two 1/2-year plus one full-year, or two full-year classes) |

EOD denotes Every Other Day.

Grade 6 Courses
Required full-year courses are ELA 6, Language Arts 6, Mathematics 6 (or another math class), Science 6, Social Studies 6, and Physical Education 6 (full year EOD). Mathematics 6 is organized in ten units: Area and Surface Area; Introducing Ratios; Linear Relationships; Unit Rates and Percentages; Dividing Fractions; Arithmetic in Base Ten; Expressions and Equations; Rational Numbers; Data Sets and Distributions; and Putting it all Together. Grade 6 electives, which meet every other day alternating with PE, are Art 6, Band 6 or Orchestra 6, and 6th Grade Choir.

Grade 7 Courses
Required courses are Digital Applications 1.0 (half year), English 7, Health and Physical Education 7 (half year), Mathematics 7 or another math class, Science 7, and Social Studies 7. Health topics include nutrition, recognizing influences, human sexuality, and choosing healthy behaviors, with information on AIDS and sexually transmitted diseases; parents may excuse their child from human sexuality and AIDS sessions. Social Studies 7 covers ancient world history and geography from the beginning of human history until around 1500.

Grade 8 Courses
Required courses are English 8, Science 8, United States History 8 (Native Americans to 1877), and a math class: Mathematics 8, Algebra 1 Honors, or Geometry Honors. Algebra 1 Honors covers five critical areas and Geometry Honors covers six; both count toward high school credit and are figured into the high school GPA.

Electives
Half-year electives for grades 7 and 8 include 2D Visual Art, 3D Visual Art, Applied Engineering, Art Expressions, Ceramics, Communication Arts, Computer Programming, Computer Science Discoveries, Creation Lab, Digital Applications 2.0, Innovation Incubator, Life Skills, LINKS (teacher recommendation only), Money Matters, Science and Engineering Explorations, Theatre Arts, Video Technology, and Video Technology 2. Full-year offerings include Chamber Orchestra, Choir 7, 7th/8th Choir, Concert Band, Graphic Design/Yearbook, Advanced Orchestra, Choir 8, Fundamentals of Fitness, Jazz Band, Physical Education (Grade 8), Symphonic Band, WEB Leadership, and World Language I in Chinese, French, German, Japanese, or Spanish.
2025_126_mscurrguide_24_25.verbose:
The Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025 is an 18-page document setting out the district's middle school philosophy, goals, student outcomes, three-year scheduling structure, and complete course descriptions for grades 6, 7, and 8. Each page carries the running footer "TSD Middle School Curriculum Guide" with the page number and "2024-2025."

Middle School Philosophy. Troy middle schools provide a program that creates an environment recognizing, accepting, respecting, and meeting the diverse needs and characteristics of young adolescent students, with a commitment to academic excellence and to being developmentally responsive to adolescents' natural characteristics: an innate curiosity, a desire to expand their environment, and the need for recognition and personal achievement. The program is characterized by a research-based curriculum with effective assessment and evaluation that is challenging, integrative, and exploratory; sharing a vision with all members of the educational community to foster respect for learning, diversity, and responsible behavior; and a cooperative partnership with parents and members of the community.

Middle School Goals. Goal 1: all programs will be developmentally appropriate. Goal 2: ensure all programs meet the needs of a diverse student population. Goal 3: ensure all students develop skills and knowledge in the core subject areas. Goal 4: provide students the opportunity to discover their special interests, attitudes, aptitudes, and abilities as the basis for determining future actions. Goal 5: provide students with diversified experiences in cultural, social, civic, vocational, and recreational programs. Goal 6: provide guidance services and programs to promote self-esteem, independence, and responsible behavior. Goal 7: provide the opportunity for students to establish partnerships with the community. Goal 8: provide a transition from elementary to high school. Goal 9: provide a model for healthy lifestyles for students.

Middle School Outcomes. In cooperative partnership with home and community, the district commits to preparing each student to become a self-directed learner who is responsible, enthusiastic, and intellectually curious; a quality worker who designs a plan, applies the best possible resources, technologies, and organizational strategies, creates products and performances, monitors development, maintains high standards, and assesses results; a positive communicator; a collaborative and cooperative contributor who creates and sustains productive group relationships; and an involved and visionary citizen who develops an awareness of global issues, contributes positively to local and world communities, advocates for the environment, and prepares to meet future challenges.

Three-Year Middle School Overview. In sixth grade all students are required to take five academic classes plus Physical Education on an every-other-day (EOD) basis; music students may add Orchestra EOD, Choir EOD, or Band EOD, and non-music students may take Art EOD. In seventh grade all students take four academic classes plus required Health/Physical Education for a half year and Digital Applications 1.0 for a half year. Seventh-grade music students take one of Concert Band (full year), Chamber Orchestra (full year), or Choir (full year), with an elective allowance totaling one full year (two half-year classes or one full-year class); non-music seventh graders take elective courses totaling one full year (two half-year electives or one full-year elective). In eighth grade all students take four academic classes; music students take one of Symphonic Band (full year), Advanced Orchestra (full year), or Choir (full year) plus an elective totaling one full year, while non-music eighth graders take a total of two full years of electives, structured as four half-year classes, two half-year classes and one full-year class, or two full-year classes.

Grade 6 required courses. ELA 6 (full year) has students study literature of various genres and informational text including literary nonfiction, with a standards-based focus on comprehension of complex texts, inferences based on textual evidence, thematic and character development, claims and evidence, academic vocabulary, and independent choice reading. Language Arts 6 (full year) covers narrative, informational, and argumentative writing using mentor texts, the writing process, conventions, short and sustained research through inquiry, and digital media presentation. Mathematics 6 (full year, required or another math class) covers ratio and rate, dividing fractions by fractions, negative numbers, and variables, organized into ten units: Unit 1 Area and Surface Area; Unit 2 Introducing Ratios; Unit 3 Linear Relationships; Unit 4 Unit Rates and Percentages; Unit 5 Dividing Fractions; Unit 6 Arithmetic in Base Ten; Unit 7 Expressions and Equations; Unit 8 Rational Numbers; Unit 9 Data Sets and Distributions; Unit 10 Putting it all Together. Physical Education 6 (full year EOD) runs either as a yearlong every-other-day program or an everyday semester class, combining cardio-respiratory fitness with games, skills development, and recreational activities. Science 6 (full year) covers life and earth science with units on cells and heredity, ecology, Earth's changing surface, and species adaptation and survival. Social Studies 6 (full year) is a geography-based course covering physical and human geography, migration and settlement, culture and cultural diffusion, population and demographic changes, resource use, trade and economic interdependence, and the responses of local, national, and international governmental and non-governmental organizations.

Grade 6 electives, which meet every other day alternating with PE, are Art 6 (elements and principles of art, comparing artwork across time and culture), Band 6 or Orchestra 6 (reinforcing fifth-grade skills; students should have taken band or orchestra in fifth grade or had formal instruction), and 6th Grade Choir (organized within the National Core Arts Standards around Perform, Create, Respond, and Connect, with day and evening performances in the schools and community).

Grade 7 courses. Digital Applications 1.0 (half year, required) explores 21st Century or Web 2.0 online tools for interactive information sharing. English 7 (full year) deepens reading comprehension, application, literary response, analysis, and vocabulary development. Health and Physical Education 7 (half year, required) is a combined ten-week course continuing the sixth-grade skill areas; health topics include nutrition, recognizing influences, human sexuality, and choosing healthy behaviors, along with countering messages encouraging tobacco, alcohol, and other drug usage and information on the spread of AIDS and sexually transmitted diseases; parents may excuse their child from class sessions covering human sexuality and AIDS. Mathematics 7 (full year, required or another math class) extends rates and ratios to equivalent ratios and proportional relationships and expands fractions to all rational numbers. Science 7 (full year) covers earth science, physics, and chemistry, including Earth's waters, weather and climate, astronomy, waves, energy, physical and chemical changes, and chemical properties. Social Studies 7 (full year) covers ancient world history and geography with a deliberate focus on content literacy, investigating human history from the beginning until around 1500, early migration and settlement patterns, and pastoral and agrarian societies leading to empires, trade networks, and diffusion of people, resources, and ideas.

Grade 8 courses. Algebra 1 Honors (full year, required or another math class) is a first-year high school algebra course for advanced students with five critical areas: linear equations and inequalities; functions including sequences interpreted graphically, numerically, symbolically, and verbally; regression techniques for approximately linear relationships; equations, inequalities, and systems involving exponential, quadratic, and rational expressions; and specialized functions including absolute value, step, and piecewise-defined functions. The course counts toward a high school credit and is figured into the high school GPA. English 8 (full year) continues study of literature of various genres and informational text. Geometry Honors (full year) is for advanced students who have completed Algebra 1 Honors and covers six critical areas: congruence in terms of rigid motions, geometric constructions, and theorems; similarity transformations and right triangle trigonometry; geometric relationships in the coordinate plane; theorems about circles; geometric measurement for two- and three-dimensional objects; and geometric concepts in modeling situations. It also counts toward a high school credit and is figured into the high school GPA. Mathematics 8 (full year) extends proportional relationships to linear relationships, linear equations in one and two variables, functions, and irrational numbers. Science 8 (full year) covers advanced earth science topics including energy, biogeochemical cycles, resources and human impacts on Earth systems, advanced rock cycle, interior of Earth, plate tectonics theory, earthquakes, volcanoes, hydrogeology, severe weather, Earth in space, the sun, Earth history and geologic time, and climate change, with cooperative lab work and an online Moodle project. United States History 8 (full year) surveys U.S. history from the time of the Native Americans to 1877, treating the American Revolution, formation of the national government, westward movement, and the Civil War and Reconstruction in detail, with periodic study of Michigan history and U.S. foreign affairs.

Grades 7 and 8 half-year electives. 2D Visual Art (painting, collage, drawing, printmaking); 3D Visual Art (papier-mache, clay, batik, mixed media); Applied Engineering (design, computer modeling, advanced manufacturing and construction, stress analysis, mechanical engineering, renewable energy systems, aerodynamics, space and rocketry); Art Expressions (ceramics, drawing, painting, sculpture, printmaking); Ceramics (pinch, coil, and slab construction, plus paper, wire, plaster, wood, and found objects); Communication Arts (public speaking, pantomime, role playing, interviews, listening skills, improvisation); Computer Programming (Introduction to JavaScript: Drawing and Animation; JavaScript: Games and Visualizations; HTML/CSS: Making Webpages; HTML/JS: Making Webpages Interactive; plus building and programming a robot); Computer Science Discoveries (problem solving, programming, physical computing, user-centered design, and data); Creation Lab (S.T.E.A.M. projects including bridge building, soldering, coding, game creation, projectiles); Digital Applications 2.0 (Adobe Creative Suite, video production, animation, digital imaging, Dreamweaver; prerequisite is successful completion of Digital Applications 1.0); Innovation Incubator (design thinking and entrepreneurship, with the cornerstone Larson Innovation Shark Tank project pitched to Metro Detroit business community members including market researchers, patent attorneys, and engineers, plus coding and 3-D printer skills); Life Skills (foods preparation and hand and machine sewing); LINKS, a peer-to-peer support program pairing general education students with students with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and other special needs, available by teacher recommendation only; Money Matters (Michigan Career Pathways, budgets, bank accounts, credit, interest, investing, responsible spending); Science and Engineering Explorations (Science and Engineering Practices, research and experimentation methodologies, the engineering and design cycle, entering work into competitions such as the Science and Engineering Fair of Metro Detroit, or SEFMD); Theatre Arts (acting, improvisation, scene study, with a public performance); Video Technology (digital video cameras, Windows Movie Maker and Apple iMovie editing, PSAs, commercials, music videos, television studio positions, daily live morning news broadcasts, media literacy and copyright ethics); and Video Technology 2, an extension of Video Technology 1.

Full-year electives. Grade 7 offerings include Chamber Orchestra (for students who successfully participated in Orchestra as a sixth grader; many evening performances required), Choir 7, 7th/8th Choir, Concert Band (continuation of sixth-grade band, placement by student proficiency, meeting daily), and Graphic Design/Yearbook, which connects students with the Boulan Park School Community and is open to seventh and eighth graders. Grade 8 offerings include 7th/8th Choir, Advanced Orchestra (for students who successfully participated in Orchestra as a seventh grader; includes a Saturday performance at the MSBOA Orchestra Festival), Choir 8, Fundamentals of Fitness, Graphic Design/Yearbook, Jazz Band (open by audition or teacher approval, previous band experience required, members also participate in a concert band ensemble), Physical Education (Grade 8), Symphonic Band (placement by proficiency, meets daily, two Saturday performances including MSBOA Band Festival), and WEB Leadership, where WEB stands for "Where Everyone Belongs" and student leaders organize school-wide initiatives such as sixth-grade orientation, character and culture programs, charity opportunities, and student mentoring. World Language I (Grade 8) is a full-year, every-day course that counts toward high school credit and is figured into the GPA; the guide notes the class may only be offered at the high school during first hour, requiring parents to provide transportation to the high school with a shuttle returning students to the middle school. The World Language I offerings are Chinese I, French I, German I, Japanese I, and Spanish I, each a full-year elective.

2025_127_m012125org_regbdmtg.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education organizational and regular meeting held January 21, 2025, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, record the annual election of officers, the adoption of standing annual resolutions, and three construction bid awards. Dr. Philippart was elected president, Mrs. Anne vice president, and Mrs. Alic secretary, each serving until December 31, 2025, with Assistant Superintendent of Business Services Dan Trudel appointed Treasurer for January through December 2025. The Board awarded $1,350,641.00 for the Troy High kitchen server project, $2,437,933.00 for the 2025 paving replacement project, and $879,465.21 for the 2025 flooring replacement project, each on a 7-0 vote.
2025_127_m012125org_regbdmtg.page:
Meeting Details
Board of Education, Troy, Michigan. Board meeting minutes for January 21, 2025, held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. Vice President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Present in addition to Mrs. Anne were Board members Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, and Zendler, along with Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Montante, Trudel, and Henry. The four high school student representatives were absent because schools were closed that day due to extreme cold temperatures. Approximately 25 members of the audience attended. The meeting was adjourned at 8:57 p.m.

Organizational Actions
Dr. Philippart was elected acting chairperson (7-0, moved by Mrs. Alic, supported by Mr. Haupt) and appointed Judy Holmes temporary secretary. Officer elections followed by roll call, all unanimous among the seven members:

| Office | Elected | Nominated by | Term |
|---|---|---|---|
| President | Dr. Philippart | Mrs. Alic | until December 31, 2025 |
| Vice President | Mrs. Anne | Mrs. Alic | until December 31, 2025 |
| Secretary | Mrs. Alic | Mr. Haupt | until December 31, 2025 |

Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, was appointed Treasurer of the Troy Board of Education for January through December 2025 (7-0). The Board adopted the resolution on Fund Depositories and Investments for January through December 2025, designating Bank of America, Citizens Bank, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Comerica Bank, Huntington Bank, Fifth Third Bank, Flagstar Bancorp, MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank), and PNC Bank. Funds may be invested according to Board Policy 5000.06, and the Treasurer may combine money from more than one fund under subsection (1)(h) of Section 380.1223 of the Revised School Code. Clark Hill, PLC, Collins & Blaha, P.C., Miller Johnson, Thrun Law Firm, P.C., and Miller Canfield were continued as legal counsel for calendar year 2025. The Superintendent was continued as Deputy Secretary, and Judy Holmes, Secretary to the Superintendent of Schools, was designated to post meeting notices. The 2025 meeting schedule and Board Committee Memberships were adopted, each 7-0.

Recognition and Reports
The TSD Mission Moment on the IA-East Capstone Experience / IB Middle Years Programme was moved to the February 25, 2025 meeting due to the school cancellation. Dr. Machesky read a statement for School Board Appreciation Month and presented gifts of appreciation. Melissa Prowse, Manager of Planning and Development for Oakland County Parks, introduced Brian Marzolf, Land Protection Manager of Six Rivers Land Conservancy, standing in for executive director Chris Bunch, who reported on Turtle Woods Nature Preserve: after an unfunded 2023 Trust Fund application, a 2024 application with increased match was awarded $2,175,000 in December, with construction projected to begin 2026-2027 for a parking lot, restrooms, trails, and boardwalks.

Business Actions

| Project | Total | Fund |
|---|---|---|
| THS Kitchen Server Project | $1,350,641.00 | Food Services Fund |
| 2025 Paving Replacement Project | $2,437,933.00 | Capital Projects Fund |
| 2025 Flooring Replacement Project | $879,465.21 | Building Site & Sinking Fund |

Consent agenda items A, B, and C (December 3, 2024 Workshop minutes, December 17, 2024 meeting minutes, and the November 2024 Treasurer's Report) were approved 7-0. Seven community members addressed the Board during public communication, with no action taken. Paul Wills of Plante Moran Realpoint presented an Attendance Area Review update, noting Phase 3 community feedback between February and April via four listening sessions and a community survey.
2025_127_m012125org_regbdmtg.verbose:
Minutes of the Troy Board of Education meeting of January 21, 2025, held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan. Vice President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, present were Board members Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, and Zendler. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Montante, Trudel, and Henry. The four high school student representatives were not in attendance because schools were closed that day due to extreme cold temperatures. Approximately 25 members of the audience were in attendance. Mrs. Anne explained that the evening's meeting is where the Board selects officers, appoints committee members for the upcoming year, and approves or authorizes items that must be considered on an annual basis, with the regular Board meeting following the organizational portion.

Election of Acting Chairperson. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt that Dr. Philippart serve as acting chairperson to officiate the meeting until the election of a president was completed. The vote was Yes: 7, No: 0.

Appointment of Temporary Secretary. Dr. Philippart appointed Judy Holmes to act as temporary secretary until the secretary of the Troy Board of Education had been elected.

Nomination and Election of President. Acting Chairperson Philippart declared nominations in order for the office of Board president. Mrs. Alic nominated Dr. Philippart. It was moved by Mrs. Potts and supported by Mrs. Anne that nominations be closed; Yes: 7, No: 0. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt that Dr. Philippart serve as president of the Troy Board of Education until December 31, 2025. On the roll call vote, Alic, Anne, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, and Zendler all voted Yes.

Nomination and Election of Vice President. President Philippart declared nominations in order for vice president. Mrs. Alic nominated Mrs. Anne. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Anne that nominations be closed; Yes: 7, No: 0. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne that Mrs. Anne serve as vice president until December 31, 2025. On the roll call vote, Anne, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, Zendler, and Alic all voted Yes.

Nomination and Election of Secretary. President Philippart declared nominations in order for secretary. Mr. Haupt nominated Mrs. Alic. It was moved by Dr. Melton and supported by Mr. Haupt that nominations be closed; Yes: 7, No: 0. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Haupt that Mrs. Alic serve as secretary until December 31, 2025. On the roll call vote, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, Zendler, Alic, and Anne all voted Yes.

Appointment of School Board Treasurer. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Haupt that Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, be appointed as Treasurer of the Troy Board of Education for the period January through December 2025. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Establish Fund Depositories and Investments. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne that the Board adopt the resolution on Fund Depositories and Investments for the period January through December 2025, with a copy of the attached resolution incorporated in its entirety as part of the official minutes. The resolution recites that public monies belonging to or held for the State, County, or other political units of the State may come into the hands of Daniel Trudel, Treasurer of Troy School District, and that under the laws of Michigan the Board is required to provide by Resolution for the deposit of all public monies, including tax monies. The Treasurer is directed to deposit and/or invest all public monies in his name as Treasurer into the following depository institutions: Bank of America; Citizens Bank; JP Morgan Chase Bank; Comerica Bank; Huntington Bank; Fifth Third Bank; Flagstar Bancorp; MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank); and PNC Bank. Monies may be withdrawn by checks signed with a facsimile signature of Treasurer Daniel Trudel, and in emergencies the handwritten signature of Daniel Trudel or Superintendent Richard M. Machesky, who may sign on the General Fund account and the Payroll account at Bank of America. Monies in the accounts established at PNC Bank for paying Troy Career Center expenses may be withdrawn by checks with the handwritten signature of the Troy Career Center Manager, Assistant Manager, or Program Coordinators. The Treasurer may open or close accounts with the listed institutions provided it is in the interest of the District. District funds may be invested according to Board Policy 5000.06, and the Treasurer is authorized to combine money from more than one fund for the purpose of making an investment authorized by subsection (1)(h) of Section 380.1223 of the Revised School Code. The maximum amount to be invested with the above institutions is regulated by the school code. The certification reads: "I, Emina Alic, Secretary of Troy School District, Oakland County, Michigan, certify that the Resolution was adopted by said Board at a meeting thereof held on the date specified above," given under hand and seal of the Troy School District in the County of Oakland in the State of Michigan this 21st day of January 2025. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Designation of Board and District Legal Counsel. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Anne to continue the designation of Clark Hill, PLC; Collins & Blaha, P.C.; Miller Johnson; Thrun Law Firm, P.C.; and Miller Canfield as legal counsel to advise and/or represent the Troy School District and Board of Education as necessary for the 2025 calendar year, with the superintendent authorized to consult additional counsel as needed with prior notification to the board. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Designation of Superintendent to be Deputy Secretary. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Dr. Melton to continue the designation of the Superintendent of Schools as Deputy Secretary of the Board with authority to act for the secretary for the 2025 calendar year. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Designation of Person for Posting Notices of Meetings. It was moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Anne that the person designated for posting notices of meetings for the 2025 calendar year shall be Judy Holmes, Secretary to the Superintendent of Schools. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Meeting Schedule and Committee Assignments. It was moved by Mrs. Potts and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Board adopt the schedule of meetings for the 2025 calendar year as indicated on the attached calendar; Yes: 7, No: 0. It was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Board adopt the Board Committee Memberships for the 2025 school year as attached; Yes: 7, No: 0.

Recognition. Dr. Machesky announced that the TSD Mission Moment on the IA-East Capstone Experience / IB Middle Years Programme had been moved to the February 25, 2025, Board of Education Meeting due to the cancellation of school that day. For Board Recognition Month, Dr. Machesky read a statement noting that each January the Troy School District honors and celebrates the trustees of its Board of Education, that School Board Appreciation Month recognizes the critical role board members play in reinforcing the district mission of ensuring learning for all, and thanking members for shaping policies, fiscal stewardship, and support of world-class teaching and learning. He then presented the members with a gift of appreciation.

Turtle Woods Update. Melissa Prowse, Manager of Planning and Development for Oakland County Parks, shared that Chris Bunch, Executive Director of Six Rivers Land Conservancy, was ill and unable to attend. She introduced Brian Marzolf, Land Protection Manager of Six Rivers Land Conservancy, who provided a report updating the community on the progress of the Turtle Woods Nature Preserve. Partners in the initiative with Oakland County Parks have been Six Rivers Land Conservancy, Troy School District, City of Troy, and Stage Nature Center. They applied to the Trust Fund in 2023 and were not funded; they applied in 2024 with increased match and were awarded $2,175,000 in December. Construction is projected to begin 2026-2027 and will include a parking lot, restrooms, trails, and boardwalks. Turtle Woods Nature Preserve will become a public park as soon as the project is complete. Dr. Machesky recognized Ida Edmunds, a Troy School District Board Member for over 30 years and a proponent of preserving the property who helped initiate the project, and also recognized former Troy School Board President Karl Schmidt, who helped push the project over the finish line.

Additions and Deletions: none. Public Communication (non-agenda items): Dr. Philippart provided the opportunity for community members to address the Board for both agenda and non-agenda items; seven community members addressed the Board during public communication and no action was taken by the Board.

Consent Agenda. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Board approve items A, B, and C on the consent agenda: minutes of the December 3, 2024, Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the December 17, 2024, Board of Education Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for November 2024. Yes: 7, No: 0. Personnel: none. Curriculum: none.

Business: THS Kitchen Server Project. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Alic that the bid for remodeling the kitchen serving area at Troy High be awarded as follows and that the amount be approved as an expenditure of the Food Services Fund: Selective Demolition, Graham Construction, $48,700.00; General Trades, Graham Construction, $219,335.00; Hard Tile, Omega Floors, $51,500.00; Food Service Equipment, Great Lakes Hotel Supply, $675,491.00; Mechanical, Quality Air Systems, $148,800.00; Electrical, Innovative Energy Controls, $206,815.00; TOTAL $1,350,641.00. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Business: 2025 Paving Replacement Project. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Anne that the bid for Site Work Paving Projects be awarded as follows and that the amount be approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund: Paving, T&M Asphalt Paving Replacement/Resurfacing, $2,193,770.00; 6% Contingency, $131,626.00; Great Lakes Landscape Design, Barnard Drainage System & Installation, $112,537.00; TOTAL $2,437,933.00. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Business: 2025 Flooring Replacement Project. It was moved by Dr. Melton and supported by Mr. Haupt that the bid for flooring replacement work be awarded as follows and that the amount be approved as an expenditure of the Building Site & Sinking Fund: Conventional Carpet, Flooring Demo/Replacement, $744,015.21; Diamond Shine Polishing, Floor Polishing, $85,450.00; Additional/Emergency Flooring, $50,000.00; TOTAL $879,465.21. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Public Communication (non-agenda items), second call: Dr. Philippart noted that he had provided an opportunity for all community members who wished to speak during the evening's meeting to address the board at the beginning of the meeting under agenda items.

Other: Attendance Area Review Update Report. Dr. Machesky introduced Paul Wills, partner at Plante Moran Realpoint, who shared a PowerPoint presentation with the Board and community providing an update on the Attendance Area Review process. He shared the background for why the process was started and the work of the group to date, discussed each phase of the process, and indicated that the district will seek community feedback in Phase 3 between February and April. TSD will hold four listening sessions for families, one at each middle school, and will send out a community survey for additional feedback. He reviewed enrollment history and projected enrollment and discussed elementary schools that are split to different middle schools, and shared Option C in more detail. Board members discussed the process and raised questions about transportation for siblings who are grandfathered in and about building utilization and current use of buildings.

Board Comments: Board members offered sentiments and comments before the close of the meeting.

Adjournment. Dr. Philippart announced that the next Board Workshop will be held on Tuesday, February 11th at 6:00 pm in the Administration Building and the next Board Meeting will be held on Tuesday, February 25th at 7:00 pm in the Services Building. The meeting was adjourned at 8:57 p.m. Respectfully submitted, Emina Alic, Secretary, Troy Board of Education. Reference notation: EA/jh.
